title: Telegram build lab
summary: A hands-on build of the Telegram side of a funnel: a private channel with named join-request links, a bot made in BotFather, a small bot that greets and approves, welcome flows, broadcasts, and a launch test. You finish with a working, tracked, consent-first setup you can point ads at.

lessons.title: Set up your channel the right way
objectives: By the end you can create a Telegram channel and choose public or private on purpose
By the end you can set a clear name, description, photo and pinned welcome post
By the end you can add admins with only the rights they need
By the end you can create one named join-request link per ad source and read the results

steps.h: Why the setup decides your costs
steps.p: Every dollar you spend on Telegram ads lands on this channel. If links are shared, you cannot tell which ad set brought members who stay, so you move budget by guesswork. If the join screen looks careless or overpromises, people hesitate, and that raises your cost per join on every ad you run.

d.b: The channel is where your ad money lands
d.s: Set it up badly and every ad pays for it

steps.text: Tap the camera circle and upload a simple square logo. A clean photo looks trustworthy in the join screen.

steps.h: Public or private for paid traffic
steps.p: A public channel has a t.me username anyone can search and open. A private channel is only reachable through invite links you create. For paid traffic most operators choose private, because every person must arrive through a link you made, and that is what lets you count joins per ad source.

a.title: Public channel
items: Good for organic growth and brand search
Cannot force join requests on the main username
Hard to tell which ad brought whom

b.title: Private channel
items: Each link can require admin approval
Each link can carry a name per ad source
Clean per-source counts for your sheet

steps.say: Now the choice. A public channel has a username anyone can search and open. It's good for organic growth and brand search, but you can't force join requests on the main username, and it's hard to tell which ad brought whom. A private channel is only reachable by invite links. Each link can require admin approval and carry a name per ad source, which gives clean per-source counts for your sheet. That's why, for paid traffic, most operators choose private.

steps.p: People decide in seconds on the join screen. The name should say what they get, not hype. The description should repeat your ad promise in plain words and include an honest line such as "education only". The photo should be simple and readable at small size.
steps.more: Message match from the Landers and Telegram module starts here. If your ad says "Free daily market notes in plain English", the channel name and description should say the same thing. When the join screen matches the ad, more people tap Request to Join. When it says something different, they hesitate and leave. Avoid promises the channel cannot keep, such as guaranteed profits or fixed daily returns. In regulated verticals like trading or gambling, the ad usually needs platform authorization and must follow local law; check both before you run.

steps.p: Your first post is the one new members see. Write it, then pin it so it stays at the top. It should say who runs the channel, what you post and how often, what the channel is not, and how to leave or mute. Pin it so it is easy to find later.

steps.p: When two ad sets share one link you can no longer tell which one brought the joins. You end up guessing. One named link per source turns the channel admin screen and your bot logs into a simple report you can copy into your daily sheet.

steps.p: Compare two links using the same spend. Cost per approved join is spend divided by approved joins. The cheaper link is not always the better one; check day-7 retention before you move budget.
steps.more: Retained members: A keeps 400 x 0.65 = 260 people. B keeps 480 x 0.40 = 192 people. Cost per retained member: A is $120 / 260 = $0.46, B is $120 / 192 = $0.63. B looked cheaper on the first day, but A is cheaper once you count the people who stayed. This is why the link name matters: without it you could not split the two.

steps.say: Let's compare two links with the same spend. Example figures. Ad set A: one hundred and twenty dollars, four hundred approved, thirty cents per join, sixty five percent still in on day seven. Ad set B: same spend, four hundred and eighty approved, twenty five cents per join, but only forty percent still in. A keeps two hundred and sixty people, B keeps one hundred and ninety two. So A costs forty six cents per retained member, and B sixty three. B looked cheaper on day one, but A is cheaper once you count who stayed.

steps.h: Link numbers and the rule card
steps.p: Joins tell you early which link is healthy, but you are paid on deposits. Use cost per retained member to compare links and warn you early. Kill and scale calls follow the rule card from the Budget and kill rules module, on network-confirmed FTDs. Starting rules; adapt them to your vertical and data.
steps.more: Example: payout $40, target cost per FTD $30, break-even $40. The CPA kill line is the lower of 1.5 × target ($45) and break-even ($40), so $40. A link whose ad set has spent $60 with 0 FTDs is killed, however cheap its joins look. A link with cheap joins and 4 FTDs at $22 each (0.73 × target) earns a +20% step, then waits at least 48 hours before the next one.

steps.say: Joins warn you early, but you're paid on deposits. In the table, cost per retained member is an early warning only. Compare links with it, never scale on it. Kill and scale calls use the rule card, on network-confirmed F T Ds, first time deposits. Zero F T Ds at spend of two times target C P A, cost per acquisition, kill. C P A over the kill line at three times target, kill. Three or more F T Ds with C P A at or under point eight times target, scale twenty percent, steps forty eight hours apart. Anything else, hold. Adapt these starting rules to your data.

steps.p: These are the setup mistakes we see most often in new funnels. Each one is cheap to avoid now and expensive to discover after a week of paid traffic, because by then the data you needed was never recorded.

a.title: Mistakes
items: One link shared by every ad set
Sharing your login with the team

b.title: Fixes
items: One named link per ad source
Plain name that matches the ad
Admins with only the rights they need

steps.say: These setup mistakes are the ones seen most often. A public channel for paid traffic, use a private channel with join-request links. One link shared by every ad set, use one named link per source. A hype name like guaranteed daily profits, use a plain name that matches the ad. Sharing your login with the team, add admins with only the rights they need. No pinned welcome post, pin an honest one before traffic. Each is cheap to avoid now, and expensive to discover after a week, because the data was never recorded.

quiz.q: Why do most operators choose a private channel for paid traffic?
options: Private channels get more reach in Telegram search
Every person must arrive through an invite link you created, so you can count joins per source
Public channels cannot have a description
quiz.why: Private channels are only reachable by your invite links, which can require approval and carry a name per source. Search reach and reporting have nothing to do with it.

quiz.q: A media buyer on your team only needs to create invite links. Which admin setup is right?
options: Turn on every right so they are never blocked
Turn on Invite users via link and leave Add new admins off
quiz.why: Give only the rights the job needs. Sharing your login or every right makes mistakes and account loss more likely.

quiz.q: Two ad sets share one invite link. What is the main problem?
options: The link stops working after 100 joins
You cannot tell which ad set brought the joins
quiz.why: A shared link mixes the sources together, so you lose the per-source counts that guide budget decisions.

quiz.q: Link A: $100 spend, 250 approved, 60% still in on day 7. Link B: $100 spend, 300 approved, 40% still in. Which costs less per retained member?
quiz.why: A keeps 150 people for $100, about $0.67 each. B keeps 120 for $100, about $0.83 each, so A is cheaper per retained member.

quiz.q: What belongs in a pinned welcome post?
options: A promise of fixed daily profits
Who runs it, what and when you post, an honest risk line, and how to leave
Only the link to the offer
A countdown that says the channel closes tonight
quiz.why: Honest expectations reduce early leaves and keep you within platform rules. Profit promises and fake countdowns are misleading.

objectives: By the end you can create a bot with @BotFather and choose a valid username
By the end you can explain what the bot token is and how to keep it secret

steps.p: Every Telegram bot is created inside one official chat called @BotFather. It is itself a bot, run by Telegram. You send it commands and it creates and edits your bots. There is no website form to fill in. Look for the verified tick next to the name so you do not open a copycat.

d.s: The only official place to create a bot

steps.say: Every Telegram bot is created inside one official chat called BotFather. It's a bot itself, run by Telegram. You send it commands, and it creates and edits your bots. There's no website form to fill in. One thing to do every time: look for the verified tick next to the name, so you don't open a copycat. BotFather is the only official place to create a bot.

steps.p: Scammers create look-alike accounts with names such as BotFather_Official or Bot Father Support. They ask for your token or a "verification fee". The real one is @BotFather with a verified badge. It never asks for money and never messages you first.

d.text: If any account asks for your bot token, payment or login code, stop. That is not BotFather.

steps.say: About those copycats. Scammers create look-alike accounts with names like BotFather underscore Official, or Bot Father Support. They ask for your token, or a verification fee. The real one is BotFather with a verified badge. It never asks for money, and it never messages you first. Read the warning: if any account asks for your bot token, payment or login code, stop. That's not BotFather.

steps.h: What a leaked token can cost
steps.p: The token is the only key to your bot, so losing it is a money problem, not just a technical one. A stranger with your token can message everyone who started the bot, act in your channel with the bot's rights and wipe out trust you paid ads to build.
steps.more: Check: 2,500 × 5% = 125 people. 125 × $0.40 = $50 of paid contacts gone in one evening, before counting members who saw the scam and left. The fix in the last lesson takes two minutes; prevention takes none.

d.text: Example: 2,500 people started your bot at about $0.40 each. A leaked token lets a stranger send them a scam link. If 5% block the bot, you lose 125 contacts, about $50 of ad spend, plus their trust.

steps.p: Beginners mix these three up. The display name is for people. The username is the bot address and must end in "bot", for example dmn_helper_bot. The token is the secret key your code or tool uses. Only the token gives control of the bot.

steps.say: Beginners often mix these three up, so look at the cards. The display name is what people see, and you can change it any time. The username is the bot's address, and it must end in bot, for example, D M N helper bot. And the token is the secret key your code or tool uses. Whoever has it controls the bot. Only the token gives control.

steps.p: A token is a number, a colon, then a long string of letters, numbers, dashes and underscores. The number before the colon is the bot ID. Treat the whole thing like a bank password. In this course we always write it as <TOKEN> so no real token is ever shown.
steps.more: Anyone holding the token can read the messages sent to the bot, send messages as the bot to everyone who started it, and, if the bot is an admin, act in your channel with the rights you gave it. That includes approving or declining join requests. Store it in a password manager or in an environment variable on your server. If you hire a developer, give them access to the server or tool, not a copy in a chat. The last lesson of this module, Test, launch and troubleshoot, shows how to replace a leaked token with /revoke.

steps.say: Most token leaks aren't hacks. They're copies the owner left in the wrong place. On the left, never here: WhatsApp or Telegram chats, screenshots and screen recordings, code pushed to a public GitHub repo, or shared spreadsheets. On the right, here: a password manager, an environment variable on your server, or the secure settings field of a tool you trust. And nowhere else.

steps.p: Here is the whole flow. A person taps your ad, then your named link. Telegram creates a join request and sends it to your bot as an update. The bot greets the person privately, approves them and logs the link name. That log is your per-source report.

The bot greets the new member privately and approves them, and it writes the link name into your join log. That log becomes your per-source report.

steps.h: Why connect a bot at all
steps.p: Without a bot, someone must approve every request by hand and nobody greets people in the short private window. At 360 requests a day that is a full-time job, and every slow approval loses people you paid for. A bot greets, approves and logs the link name in seconds, every time.

Never give a bot Add new admins: if the token ever leaks, the attacker could add more admins and take the channel. In the Bot API this permission is called can_invite_users, and it is the one approveChatJoinRequest checks.

steps.p: A bot learns about new events in one of two ways. With long polling, your program keeps asking Telegram "anything new?" With a webhook, Telegram calls your server when something happens. Both work. You use one at a time, never both.
steps.more: Long polling: the program calls getUpdates with a timeout, for example 30 seconds. Telegram holds the call open until there is an update or the time runs out, then the program asks again. You pass offset = last update_id + 1 so Telegram knows which updates you already handled. Webhook: you call setWebhook once with your HTTPS URL. At the time of writing Telegram only sends to ports 443, 80, 88 or 8443. While a webhook is set, getUpdates is refused with a 409 Conflict error. Call deleteWebhook to go back to polling.

items: Your program asks Telegram in a loop
Runs on a laptop or small server
Best for learning and small bots

b.title: Webhook (setWebhook)
items: Telegram sends updates to your URL
Better for many bots or busy bots

It needs a public H T T P S address, suits many or busy bots, and is used by most hosted tools. Both work. Use one at a time, never both.

steps.h: Worked example: when the bot is down
steps.p: Downtime does not lose join requests. They stay pending. But the greeting window is short, so people who requested while the bot was off get approved later without a greeting. That costs you the chance to invite them to start the bot.
steps.more: The 30% Start rate is an example only. The fix is cheap: run the bot on a small always-on server or use a hosted tool, and add an alert if the bot stops. Some operators also review pending requests by hand when a bot was down, from the channel Subscribers or Requests screen.

d.text: Example. 360 requests a day, about 15 an hour. The bot is off for 6 hours overnight, so about 90 requests pile up. When it restarts it can still approve all 90, but at the time of writing their 5-minute window has passed, so it cannot greet them. If 30% of greeted people tap Start, you lose about 27 bot contacts that day.

steps.p: When a join flow breaks, it is usually one of these five mistakes. None of them shows an obvious error on the channel itself. You only notice them when greetings, approvals or Start counts stop adding up in your log.

Polling and a webhook at the same time
Bot on a laptop that sleeps

steps.say: Plan the send time before you press go. The equation is simple. Recipients, divided by messages per second, equals seconds to send. And here's the important part: use a rate below the limit, not at it. That leaves room for retries and for the bot's other traffic.

steps.p: Work out the send time and whether it fits your posting slot. A queue that runs below the limit is slower but avoids 429 errors and failed sends.
steps.more: Also count what the send costs you in goodwill. Example: if 0.5% of recipients block the bot after each promo broadcast, that is 60 people per send from 12,000. Ten promo sends a month would lose about 600 people. Compare that with the conversions those sends bring before you decide how often to promote. These figures are an example only; track your own block rate per broadcast.

d.text: Example. 12,000 active members in segment NG_NEW. Safe rate 25 messages per second. 12,000 / 25 = 480 seconds, so 8 minutes. Start at 7:55am to finish by 8:03am. If 300 return error 403, remove those 300 now; your active list becomes 11,700.

steps.p: Turn block rates into rules you apply after every promo send. Block rate is blocks (403 errors on the next send) divided by people messaged. These are starting rules from experience, not Telegram numbers; adapt them to your audience and vertical.

Two copies of the bot running, one receiver per token. Judging ad sets on day-one joins, use the rule card on network F T Ds. Fixing three things at once, make one fix, then retest. Each fix costs minutes, not money.

takeaways: Test the whole path from a second, non-admin account before any ad goes live.
Most failures are admin rights, approval off, wrong token, two receivers, or a user who never started the bot.
Log error_code and description; match on the code first.
If a token leaks, /revoke it in BotFather, update your server and check for damage.

glossary.def: Running the full path a real person takes, from ad link to bot reply and opt-out, before launch.
A BotFather command that cancels the current token and issues a new one.
getUpdates was refused because a webhook is set or another program is polling the same token.

quiz.q: Why test from a second account instead of the channel owner account?
options: The owner account cannot open links
The second account sees exactly what a new, non-admin person sees
Bots only work on second phones
quiz.why: An admin or owner skips parts of the join flow. A non-admin account experiences the real path.

quiz.q: People join the channel instantly and the bot never greets them. What is the most likely cause?
options: The link they used does not have Request admin approval switched on
quiz.why: Without approval on the link, there is no join request, so the bot gets no chat_join_request update to act on.

quiz.q: You pasted your token in a freelancer chat. What do you do first?
options: Send /revoke in BotFather, then update your server or tool with the new token
Delete the chat message and carry on
quiz.why: Deleting the message does not undo a copy. Revoking makes the old token useless immediately.

quiz.q: Launch day: 400 requests, 395 approved, 160 greeted. Using the health rules, what do you do first?
options: Kill the ad set behind the link
Pause ads to that link and check whether two programs are receiving updates for the bot
Raise the budget to get more data
quiz.why: 160 ÷ 400 = 40% greeted, far under the 90% health line. Pause ads to that link and fix the bot; two receivers on one token is a classic cause. The ad set is not judged until the plumbing works.

quiz.q: A bot in a group does not see normal messages. Will turning off privacy mode fix missing channel join requests?
options: Yes, privacy mode blocks join requests
Yes, but only for private channels
No, privacy mode only affects what a bot sees in groups
No, privacy mode only affects webhooks
quiz.why: Privacy mode controls which group messages a bot receives. Join requests depend on admin rights and approval links.

lessons.say_intro: Before any ad goes live, you test the whole chain yourself. In this lesson you'll run an end-to-end test, match common bot errors to fixes, replace a leaked token, and read launch-day numbers to spot a broken step.

Your task: run the full second-account test on your build, fill in the symptom-to-fix table with anything you hit, and practise revoke on your test bot. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You run Meta ads in Nigeria and Kenya to one channel using one invite link. After a week you cannot tell which geo is cheaper per retained member. What should you have done?
options: Created one named join-request link per geo and ad set
Asked members where they came from
exam.why: Named links per source give clean counts per geo and ad set without guessing or surveys.

exam.q: A new media buyer asks for your Telegram login so they can create invite links. What is the right move?
options: Add them as admin with only Invite users via link turned on
exam.why: Give each person their own admin role with the minimum rights. Sharing logins risks the whole account.

exam.q: Yesterday link META_KE_ADSET_B greeted 60% of its requests. Its ad set spent $45, target CPA $30, 0 FTDs. What is the right first move?
options: Kill the ad set: it has no FTDs
Pause ads to that link and fix the bot; $45 is still under the $60 zero-FTD kill line
Scale it, because joins are cheap
Delete the channel and start again
exam.why: Greeted under 90% is a health-rule breach, so fix the plumbing first. On the rule card, $45 is 1.5 × target with 0 FTDs, under the 2 × kill line, so the ad set is a Hold until the build works.

exam.q: You spend $150 on link A: 500 approved, 70% retained on day 7. Link B: $150, 600 approved, 45% retained. Where does the next $100 go, all else equal?
options: Link B, because it has more joins
Link A, about $0.43 per retained member against about $0.56 for B
exam.why: A keeps 350 members for $150, about $0.43 each. B keeps 270, about $0.56 each. A is cheaper per member who stays.

exam.q: Your example bot approves first and then tries to send the greeting. Most greetings fail. Why?
options: The private window closes once the request is handled, so the greeting must go first
The bot lacks Post messages right
exam.why: At the time of writing user_chat_id can be used only until the request is processed and for a short time. Greet, then approve.

exam.q: You tested a hosted join tool last month and today your own polling script gets 409 Conflict. What do you do?
options: Check getWebhookInfo and deleteWebhook, accepting this disconnects the tool, or use a separate bot for your script
Wait for Telegram to fix it
exam.why: A webhook left by the tool blocks getUpdates. One bot can feed one receiver; delete the webhook or use another bot.

exam.q: You want to broadcast to 15,000 active members at a safe 25 messages per second. When should you start to finish around 8:00am?
options: About 7:50am, since it takes about 10 minutes
exam.why: 15,000 / 25 = 600 seconds, so about 10 minutes. Starting near 7:50am finishes around 8:00am.

exam.q: A promo broadcast went to 10,000 people and the next send returned 150 new 403 errors. Using the lesson's starting rules, what do you do?
options: Send the same promo again to reach the rest
Stop promos and review what you sent: 1.5% is over the 1% line
exam.why: 150 ÷ 10,000 = 1.5% block rate, above the 1% starting line, so promos stop until the content is reviewed. Remove the 150 blocked users from your lists.

exam.q: A token was in a GitHub repo that was public for two days. You sent /revoke. What else should you check?
options: Channel admins, recent bot messages and any unknown webhook via getWebhookInfo
exam.why: Revoking stops future use. You still need to look for anything the attacker changed while they had access.

exam.q: Launch numbers for one link: 600 requests, 590 approved, 300 greeted, and sendMessage logs show many 403 errors. Which explanation fits best?
options: The bot is not an admin
Greetings are sent after approval or too late, so the window has closed and Telegram refuses them
exam.why: Approvals work, so admin rights and the link are fine. 403 on greetings means the bot is outside the window; check the order and speed of handling.
